name: git rm
shortDescription: Remove files from the working tree and the staging area. Stages the removal so it will be recorded in the next commit.
detailedDescription:
The `git rm` command removes files from both your working directory and the Git staging area (index) in a single step. It's the Git-aware equivalent of deleting a file with `rm` and then running `git add` to stage the deletion.

The most common use case for `git rm` beyond simple deletion is `--cached`: removing a file from Git tracking while keeping it on disk. This is essential when you accidentally committed a file that should have been in `.gitignore` (like `.env`, `node_modules`, or build artifacts).

After running `git rm`, you still need to commit the change to record the deletion in history. The file's content is still preserved in older commits and can be recovered if needed.

parameters.description: One or more file paths or glob patterns to remove. Required.
Remove the file from the staging area and stop tracking it, but keep the file in your working directory. The file becomes 'untracked'. This is the key flag for undoing accidental tracking.
Recursive removal. Required when removing directories. Without this flag, git rm refuses to remove directories.
Override the up-to-date check. Required when the file has local modifications that haven't been committed, to prevent accidental data loss.
Don't actually remove anything. Just show what would be removed. Useful when using glob patterns.

examples.title: Remove a file from repo and disk
examples.description: Delete a file and stage the deletion for the next commit.
examples.code:
git rm old-feature.js
git commit -m "Remove deprecated old feature"

examples.title: Stop tracking a file but keep it locally
examples.description: The most common real-world use. You committed .env or node_modules by mistake and want to untrack it without deleting it.
examples.code:
# Stop tracking .env (keep the file on disk)
git rm --cached .env

# Add it to .gitignore so it stays untracked
echo '.env' >> .gitignore

# Commit both changes
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env, add to gitignore"

examples.title: Untrack an entire directory
examples.description: Remove a directory like node_modules or dist from tracking.
examples.code:
git rm -r --cached node_modules/
echo 'node_modules/' >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Remove node_modules from tracking"

commonMistakes.text: Without `--cached`, `git rm` DELETES the file from your disk. Make sure you mean it. If you only want to stop tracking, always use `--cached`.

Even after `git rm`, the file still exists in your Git history. Anyone who clones the repo can see it in old commits. For sensitive data like passwords, you need `git filter-branch` or BFG Repo-Cleaner to purge it from history.
If you simply deleted a file with `rm` (not `git rm`), the deletion shows as 'Changes not staged'. Run `git add <deleted-file>` or `git rm <deleted-file>` to stage it.
